- Stated policy that "40% to 50% of the profits generated to be used for paying down debt, invest in new strategic initiatives and rewarding shareholders", with free cash from the capital-light strategy used "to reward shareholders via dividends over time".
- Rs 1,525 Mn dividend paid out during FY26; FY26 dividend (to be paid during FY27) of Rs 2,582 Mn, a payout of ~20%.

bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Gold price volatility — Gold climbed 44.4% to historic highs exceeding USD 5,000 per ounce on central bank purchases and dollar concerns, before a stronger dollar and rising interest rate expectations triggered a price correction. The MD&A states that such volatility presents distinct structural hurdles for retail operations, with discretionary demand for gifting and fashion items frequently pausing as cautious consumers defer purchases until pricing stabilises. The governance section notes a comprehensive gold hedging framework to manage this exposure.
- Currency depreciation raising the landed cost of imported gold — International gold prices put pressure on the INR, directly impacting the domestic supply chain, and the rupee faced downward pressure by April 2026 due to global risk aversion and rising crude oil prices, which the MD&A links explicitly to the landed cost of imported gold.
- Inventory intensity and the need for constant inventory agility — The MD&A states retailers must maintain high inventory agility across ticket sizes and carat preferences, holding a robust presence of SKUs within high-traction price bands tailored to specific micro-markets; maintaining the right showroom inventory mix during sharp gold price surges is described as critical for FY27. Mitigations disclosed are an ERP system giving real-time inventory visibility, ERP-enabled barcode tracking of every jewellery item, multi-level verification through daily stock checks and regular audits by regional managers and business heads, and integrated operations allowing inventory movement between showrooms.
- Consumer down-trading to lighter grammage within fixed budgets — Inflationary pressure on precious metals led some consumers to seek lighter-weight pieces within fixed budgets; capturing that demand required collaboration with advanced manufacturers and investment in the latest design technology to optimise gold content through lightweight designs, which is a continuing mix and margin exposure.
- Concentration of demand in weddings and festivals — Wedding and bridal demand accounts for more than 60% of total annual purchases and bridal jewellery is described as the market's primary pillar, with seasonal demand anchored on Akshaya Tritiya, Dhanteras, Durga Puja and Karva Chauth. Demand is therefore compressed into a narrow calendar, and a weak wedding or festive window is difficult to recover.
- Intensifying competition from a fragmenting set of retail formats — The market has consolidated into five distinct operational formats — national brands, regional strongholds, technology- and AI-led omnichannel specialists offering 'accessible luxury' to Millennial and Gen Z buyers, premium experiential boutiques, and international luxury houses with a growing presence in major metros — each competing for a different customer segment.
- Geopolitical and macroeconomic shocks — The MD&A describes renewed geopolitical shocks and prolonged friction in the Middle East, maritime navigation disruptions with oil fluctuating near USD 105, and global growth slowing from 3.4% in 2025 to 3.1% in 2026 — conditions the report says demanded constant operational balancing from jewellery retailers.
- Regulatory and compliance exposure in a rapidly formalising industry — Mandatory hallmarking, certified purity and pricing-transparency requirements are reshaping the industry; the Company relies on a formal Risk Management Policy and Risk Management Committee, an internal control framework reviewed at periodic intervals, a Whistle-blower/vigil mechanism reporting to the Audit Committee, and quarterly internal audit review. The Board records that no risks in its opinion threaten the existence of the Company, while noting that some risks may pose challenges as set out in the MD&A.

outlook.title: Strategy & capital allocation

outlook.body: Kalyan Jewellers' expansion is retail-footprint rather than plant capex, and is executed almost entirely through the capital-light franchise (FOCO) route. In FY26 the Company launched 129 showrooms across the Kalyan and Candere formats, entered international territory with its first showroom in the United Kingdom, and took the global showroom count to 507 as of 31 March 2026, of which 466 showrooms are in India. Non-metro markets comprise 73% of the standalone Indian showroom network, and this deep penetration is powered by the grassroots 'My Kalyan' outreach network of 1,139 centres and 4,375 dedicated personnel focused on lead generation, customer outreach and doorstep engagement without holding retail inventory. Merchandising reach is supported by 15 procurement centres strategically placed across primary manufacturing hubs. A new regional brand is being prepared for launch in FY27, offering affordable, community-specific staple jewellery crafted to mirror local traditions and regional heritage, aimed at unlocking rural and semi-urban India; the strategic-priorities pages add that the first regional brand is to be launched in FY27 and that the Company will explore the FOCO model for the new format. The stated FY27 focus is to keep accelerating network expansion through the asset-light FOCO model, expand the Candere network through a mix of COCO and FOCO showrooms, further expand the My Kalyan network, and drive robust same-store-sales growth. No rupee capex quantum, project cost, plant or installed-capacity disclosure appears in this bundle.

outlook.body:
- Accelerating formalisation of the Indian jewellery sector — regulatory reform, mandatory hallmarking, certified purity and pricing transparency are shifting share from the unorganised to the organised market, which management calls the Company's largest structural tailwind
- Cultural, largely non-discretionary demand: wedding and bridal purchases account for more than 60% of total annual purchases and bridal jewellery is the market's primary pillar, giving demand an 'inelastic' floor through the wedding calendar, festivals and rural harvest cycles
- Gold price volatility as the main swing factor — 24K gold averaged ₹1,23,000 per 10 grams in 2025 and surged to a record average of ₹1,53,150 by April 2026, with gold up 44.4% to historic highs exceeding USD 5,000 per ounce; discretionary gifting and fashion demand pauses as consumers defer purchases until pricing stabilises
- Consumer trade-down to lighter grammage within fixed budgets, which organised jewellers captured by optimising gold content through innovative lightweight designs and advanced design technology
- Premiumisation and mix shift — growing demand for lightweight jewellery, contemporary designs and diamond-studded collections alongside traditional bridal, with a higher studded share as a gross-margin lever
- Regional demand concentration: South India accounts for nearly 40% of national demand, West 25%, North 20% and East 15%, making hyperlocal assortment and marketing the decisive growth strategy
- Tier II, Tier III and rural markets as the next demand wave, where organised penetration remains relatively low despite significant consumption potential, driven by rising incomes, infrastructure development and brand awareness
- Omnichannel behaviour — consumers increasingly begin the purchase journey online and complete it in store, particularly younger, digitally native buyers who prioritise accessibility and retail experience over price-centric models
- Supportive Indian macro: real GDP growth estimated at 7.7% for FY26 on thriving urban consumption, reviving private investment and 14.5% higher government capital expenditure, creating a favourable ecosystem for consumer-facing industries
- Global backdrop of modest recalibration — IMF projects global growth slowing from 3.4% in 2025 to 3.1% in 2026 before 3.2% in 2027, with rupee pressure from global risk aversion and rising crude prices raising the landed cost of imported gold
- Industry outlook for FY27: domestic demand driven by consumer disposable income and near-term budgets, with operational agility on showroom inventory mix during sharp gold price surges described as critical
- The India jewellery market was valued at USD 95.10 Billion in 2025 and is projected to reach USD 151.37 Billion by 2034, a 5.30% CAGR over 2026-2034 (source cited as imarcgroup.com)

currentContext.expansion: Kalyan Jewellers' expansion is retail-footprint rather than plant capex, and is executed almost entirely through the capital-light franchise (FOCO) route. In FY26 the Company launched 129 showrooms across the Kalyan and Candere formats, entered international territory with its first showroom in the United Kingdom, and took the global showroom count to 507 as of 31 March 2026, of which 466 showrooms are in India. Non-metro markets comprise 73% of the standalone Indian showroom network, and this deep penetration is powered by the grassroots 'My Kalyan' outreach network of 1,139 centres and 4,375 dedicated personnel focused on lead generation, customer outreach and doorstep engagement without holding retail inventory. Merchandising reach is supported by 15 procurement centres strategically placed across primary manufacturing hubs. A new regional brand is being prepared for launch in FY27, offering affordable, community-specific staple jewellery crafted to mirror local traditions and regional heritage, aimed at unlocking rural and semi-urban India; the strategic-priorities pages add that the first regional brand is to be launched in FY27 and that the Company will explore the FOCO model for the new format. The stated FY27 focus is to keep accelerating network expansion through the asset-light FOCO model, expand the Candere network through a mix of COCO and FOCO showrooms, further expand the My Kalyan network, and drive robust same-store-sales growth. one-line thesis: Kalyan Jewellers delivered exceptional Q4FY26 with 66% revenue and 118% PAT growth, driven by robust non-South expansion and a sharp turnaround in Candere profitability. The strategic pivot to a capital-light FOCO model and imminent elimination of non-GML debt in India positions the company for sustained ROCE expansion despite high gold price volatility.
financial scorecard: Revenue: INR 10,275 Cr (+66% YoY); EBITDA/PBT: INR 539 Cr (+115% YoY); PAT: INR 410 Cr (+118% YoY); Order Book: N/A (Retail); Net Debt: Non-GML reduced by INR 360 Cr in FY26 to ~INR 300 Cr, targeting zero in FY27. One-offs: Interest cost inflated by ~INR 30 Cr due to advance tax interest and timing of debt repayments in H1.
guidance: Revenue Growth: High teens to 20%+ implied by 150 new stores; Margin: India PBT ~5.5-5.6%, Candere GM mid-30s; Order Inflow: Strong Akshaya Tritiya start; Capex: Minimal for FOCO, focused on inventory for COCO/hybrid.
order book & pipeline: N/A - Retail business model relies on same-store sales growth (SSSG) and new store ramp-ups rather than traditional order books. Current SSSG trends >20% in recent quarters.
segment / subsidiary detail: India: Rev INR 8,990 Cr (+68%), PAT INR 366 Cr (+97%). Middle East: Rev INR 1,074 Cr (+37%), PAT INR 21 Cr. Candere: Rev INR 131 Cr (+368%), turned PAT positive (INR 3 Cr vs loss of INR 12 Cr).
growth verticals / optionality: 150 new stores planned in FY27 (50-55 Candere, rest Kalyan); Potential conversion of Middle East FOCO to franchisee model unlocking ~INR 800-1000 Cr cash flow; New regional brand launch pending political clarity in target state.
margins & cost dynamics: India gross margins pressured by mix (FOCO vs COCO) and seasonality; Candere commands mid-30% GM due to >70% studded mix. FY26 GM benefited from silver/platinum tailwinds (~INR 20 Cr) which are non-recurring. Operating leverage expected to offset commodity mix headwinds.
capex / expansion: Capital light strategy via FOCO (Franchisee Owned, Company Operated). Capex primarily for COCO renovations, hybrid store upgrades, and inventory funding. Free cash flow prioritized for debt reduction and dividends.
capital allocation: 50% of cash flow allocated to dividends (20% payout ratio declared) and debt reduction; 50% reserved for Candere expansion, new regional brand, and inventory buildup. Target: Zero non-GML debt in India by FY27.
risks & watch-items: Gold price volatility suppressing volume growth; Adhik-Maas (leap month) causing Q1 wedding demand shift; Geopolitical tension affecting Middle East operations; Execution risk on new regional brand launch.
management quality / tone: Confident and pragmatic; Emphasizes volume discipline over value growth during high gold price regimes; Cautious on guiding specific SSSG numbers despite strong momentum; Transparent on one-off interest costs.
non-obvious takeaways: Management explicitly guides to conservative 10% SSSG for long-term modeling despite 20-30% recent runs to manage expectations; Volume growth is actively managed by shifting customers to lower karat (18K/14K) and studded jewelry as gold prices rise, preserving revenue despite lower gram sales.

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- Accelerating formalisation of the Indian jewellery sector — regulatory reform, mandatory hallmarking, certified purity and pricing transparency are shifting share from the unorganised to the organised market, which management calls the Company's largest structural tailwind
- Cultural, largely non-discretionary demand: wedding and bridal purchases account for more than 60% of total annual purchases and bridal jewellery is the market's primary pillar, giving demand an 'inelastic' floor through the wedding calendar, festivals and rural harvest cycles
- Gold price volatility as the main swing factor — 24K gold averaged ₹1,23,000 per 10 grams in 2025 and surged to a record average of ₹1,53,150 by April 2026, with gold up 44.4% to historic highs exceeding USD 5,000 per ounce; discretionary gifting and fashion demand pauses as consumers defer purchases until pricing stabilises
- Consumer trade-down to lighter grammage within fixed budgets, which organised jewellers captured by optimising gold content through innovative lightweight designs and advanced design technology
- Premiumisation and mix shift — growing demand for lightweight jewellery, contemporary designs and diamond-studded collections alongside traditional bridal, with a higher studded share as a gross-margin lever
- Regional demand concentration: South India accounts for nearly 40% of national demand, West 25%, North 20% and East 15%, making hyperlocal assortment and marketing the decisive growth strategy
- Tier II, Tier III and rural markets as the next demand wave, where organised penetration remains relatively low despite significant consumption potential, driven by rising incomes, infrastructure development and brand awareness
- Omnichannel behaviour — consumers increasingly begin the purchase journey online and complete it in store, particularly younger, digitally native buyers who prioritise accessibility and retail experience over price-centric models
- Supportive Indian macro: real GDP growth estimated at 7.7% for FY26 on thriving urban consumption, reviving private investment and 14.5% higher government capital expenditure, creating a favourable ecosystem for consumer-facing industries
- Global backdrop of modest recalibration — IMF projects global growth slowing from 3.4% in 2025 to 3.1% in 2026 before 3.2% in 2027, with rupee pressure from global risk aversion and rising crude prices raising the landed cost of imported gold
- Industry outlook for FY27: domestic demand driven by consumer disposable income and near-term budgets, with operational agility on showroom inventory mix during sharp gold price surges described as critical
- The India jewellery market was valued at USD 95.10 Billion in 2025 and is projected to reach USD 151.37 Billion by 2034, a 5.30% CAGR over 2026-2034 (source cited as imarcgroup.com)

margins.title: Margins & cost dynamics
margins.body: India gross margins pressured by mix (FOCO vs COCO) and seasonality; Candere commands mid-30% GM due to >70% studded mix. FY26 GM benefited from silver/platinum tailwinds (~INR 20 Cr) which are non-recurring. Operating leverage expected to offset commodity mix headwinds.

capital_allocation.title: Capital allocation
capital_allocation.body: 50% of cash flow allocated to dividends (20% payout ratio declared) and debt reduction; 50% reserved for Candere expansion, new regional brand, and inventory buildup. Target: Zero non-GML debt in India by FY27.

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: Kalyan Jewellers' expansion is retail-footprint rather than plant capex, and is executed almost entirely through the capital-light franchise (FOCO) route. In FY26 the Company launched 129 showrooms across the Kalyan and Candere formats, entered international territory with its first showroom in the United Kingdom, and took the global showroom count to 507 as of 31 March 2026, of which 466 showrooms are in India. Non-metro markets comprise 73% of the standalone Indian showroom network, and this deep penetration is powered by the grassroots 'My Kalyan' outreach network of 1,139 centres and 4,375 dedicated personnel focused on lead generation, customer outreach and doorstep engagement without holding retail inventory. Merchandising reach is supported by 15 procurement centres strategically placed across primary manufacturing hubs. A new regional brand is being prepared for launch in FY27, offering affordable, community-specific staple jewellery crafted to mirror local traditions and regional heritage, aimed at unlocking rural and semi-urban India; the strategic-priorities pages add that the first regional brand is to be launched in FY27 and that the Company will explore the FOCO model for the new format. The stated FY27 focus is to keep accelerating network expansion through the asset-light FOCO model, expand the Candere network through a mix of COCO and FOCO showrooms, further expand the My Kalyan network, and drive robust same-store-sales growth. No rupee capex quantum, project cost, plant or installed-capacity disclosure appears in this bundle.

management_tone.title: Management quality / tone
management_tone.body: Confident and pragmatic; Emphasizes volume discipline over value growth during high gold price regimes; Cautious on guiding specific SSSG numbers despite strong momentum; Transparent on one-off interest costs.

moat.title: Bull — competitive strengths
moat.body:
- Strong brand recognition — a trusted national brand combining nationwide appeal with sharp sensitivity to hyperlocal tastes and regional sensibilities, building lasting customer loyalty across India
- Hyperlocal operating model — state- and city-specific campaigns with local brand ambassadors and regional influencers, communication in local languages, and showrooms staffed with local talent who understand regional sensibilities
- Extensive retail network across major metros, smaller cities and rural markets — 342 Kalyan showrooms in India, 38 in the Middle East, 2 in the United States and 1 in the United Kingdom as of 31 March 2026
- Grassroots 'My Kalyan' outreach network of 1,139 centres and 4,375 dedicated personnel, described as a distinct competitive strength for reaching the hinterland more efficiently than other brands
- Diverse product portfolio spanning grand traditional wedding sets to stylish lightweight everyday wear, covering every taste, occasion and budget
- Integrated digital ecosystem — Candere.com works together with physical showrooms to offer a smooth omni-channel experience
- Capital-light FOCO (Franchise Owned Company Operated) model in which franchise partners fund store setup and inventory while the Company retains operational and brand control; 222 of the 342 India Kalyan showrooms are FOCO formats and all recent fresh showroom additions follow the FOCO framework
- Supply-chain depth — 15 procurement centres placed across primary manufacturing hubs, sourcing directly from local artisans
- Strong governance — a diverse and experienced Board guided by an Independent Chairman
- Positioned to benefit from formalisation of the Indian jewellery market: the Company reports a ~7% share of the organised jewellery market (the SWOT section separately cites a 3% share of the total market and an 8% share of the organised segment)

risks.title: Risks & watch-items
risks.body: Gold price volatility suppressing volume growth; Adhik-Maas (leap month) causing Q1 wedding demand shift; Geopolitical tension affecting Middle East operations; Execution risk on new regional brand launch.

non_obvious.title: Non-obvious takeaways
non_obvious.body: Management explicitly guides to conservative 10% SSSG for long-term modeling despite 20-30% recent runs to manage expectations; Volume growth is actively managed by shifting customers to lower karat (18K/14K) and studded jewelry as gold prices rise, preserving revenue despite lower gram sales.

strategy.title: Strategies (RHP)
strategy.body:
- Scale responsibly through the capital-efficient, asset-light FOCO (Franchisee-Owned, Company-Operated) model rather than simply expanding, so the network grows without proportionate balance-sheet investment and returns on capital stay healthy
- Build a future-ready multi-brand platform — flagship Kalyan for national trust and scale, digital-first Candere for the lifestyle and youth-driven segment, and a new regional brand offering exclusively localised designs — to serve distinct age profiles, budgets and lifestyle preferences
- Pair disciplined expansion with the grassroots 'My Kalyan' outreach …

other.title: Notable from the deck
other.body:
- [Credit rating] Rating progression shown as A+ (Stable) in FY2023 and FY2024, enhanced to A+ (Positive) in FY2025 and to AA- (Stable) in FY2026, with "[f]urther enhancement expected" in FY2027.
- [Guidance] "Target same stores sales growth of mid to high single digits" is the stated same-store growth ambition.
- [Gold sourcing] Share of recycled gold in India stood at 46% during Q1FY27, versus 30% in Q1FY26 and 31% in Q4FY26; gross margin was said to be impacted by the higher proportion of exchanged gold and promotional offers under the exchange campaign.
- [One-off] "~Rs 41 Cr one-off gain from import duty hike during the quarter" (India), and a Rs 415 Mn exceptional item recognised due to changes in employee benefit provisions arising from the New Labour Codes.
- [Ownership history] Warburg Pincus invested equity in 2014 with an incremental investment in 2017; the company listed on NSE & BSE via IPO in 2021 and a Warburg Pincus MD (Anish Kumar Saraf) sits on the Board as a Non-Executive Director.
